did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter presents Job as blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil—a description that highlights his moral and spiritual character from the beginning of the story.
Did you know? Job had ten children: seven sons and three daughters.

Did you know? Job’s wealth included seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, as well as many servants. For this reason, he is described as the greatest of all the people of the East.

Did you know? After his children’s days of feasting, Job would rise early and offer burnt offerings for all of them, fearing that they might have sinned in their hearts. According to the text, he did this continually.
Did you know? The chapter describes a scene in which the sons of God present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also comes among them.
Did you know? The LORD Himself testifies that there is no one like Job on earth: he is blameless and upright, fears God, and turns away from evil.
Did you know? Satan argues that Job’s fear of God may not be without reward, but may be connected to the blessings, protection, and wealth the LORD has given him.
Did you know? The LORD allows Satan to strike everything Job has, but commands him not to touch Job himself.
Did you know? The disasters strike Job one after another while his sons and daughters are eating and drinking in their oldest brother’s house.

Did you know? The messengers report four kinds of disaster: the Sabeans raiding the oxen and donkeys, fire striking the sheep, the Chaldeans raiding the camels, and finally a great wind collapsing the house on Job’s children.
Did you know? In response to the disasters, Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships—profound expressions of mourning that appear together in the chapter.
Did you know? Despite losing his possessions and children, the chapter concludes that Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.
